title: Judicial Independence & Accountability
lead: The SC recognised ==Independence of the Judiciary as basic structure== in [[SC AoR Assn v. UoI (1994)]] — but ==judicial accountability== remains a delicate balance between parliamentary democracy and public trust. ==8,630 complaints against judges between 2016–2025== (Law Minister's reply to a parliamentary question).

items.title: Structural / Institutional
bullets: ==Separation of powers== — judges outside legislature/executive (==Art 50==)
==Security of tenure== — removal only by impeachment (Arts 124(4), 217)
==Financial autonomy== — salaries on the Consolidated Fund, not variable to a judge's disadvantage (Arts 125, 221)
==Collegium primacy== in appointments and transfers (2nd & 3rd Judges cases)
Fixed service conditions

items.title: Functional
bullets: ==No interference in judicial functions== (Art 141)
Control over procedure, contempt, listing
==Arts 121 & 211== bar discussion of a judge's conduct in legislatures except on impeachment; ==Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968==
Parliament may ==add to but not curtail== SC powers
==Contempt power== (Arts 129/215)

items.title: Internal
bullets: Freedom from influence ==within== the judiciary — including pressure from Chief Justices

items.title: Decisional
bullets: Judges decide ==‘without fear or favour, affection or ill-will’== — Third Schedule oath

items.title: Constitutional
bullets: ==Impeachment== for ‘proved misbehaviour or incapacity’ — Arts 124(4), 217(1)(b)
==Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968==: motion by ==100 LS or 50 RS== members, three-member committee, ==two-thirds majority== in both Houses
Declaration of assets — ==SC Resolution (1997)==, not binding
==Art 235==: HC control over the subordinate judiciary

items.title: Institutional
bullets: ==In-House Procedure== for internal inquiry into complaints
[[K. Veeraswami v. UoI (1991)]]: ==prior CJI permission== needed to investigate judges
==Restatements of Judicial Values (1999)== — an ethical code

items.title: Public
bullets: ==Reasoned judgments== as public documents, open to appeal and academic scrutiny
[[CPIO, SC v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (2010)]] — RTI on a ==case-by-case basis==
==Contempt of court== — protects dignity, but excessive use can ==stifle legitimate criticism==

items.title: Case Studies
bullets: ==Justice V. Ramaswami== — impeachment failed in 1993 due to political abstentions
==Justice Soumitra Sen== resigned before completion; ==Justice Dinakaran== resigned on the day of inquiry
==Justice Varma (Delhi HC)== currently in the news; ==Justice Gogoi== (conflict of interest)

items: ==High threshold for removal== — the 100/50-member motion, committee inquiry and two-thirds majority make removal ==extremely rare==.
==Political influence and delay== — the process is susceptible to partisan derailment.
==No intermediate sanctions== — no censure, suspension or lesser penalty: the process is ==all-or-nothing==.
==In-house mechanism limits== — no statutory backing, no transparency, decisions not disclosed.
==Resignation as a loophole== — judges resign to halt investigation and escape accountability.
==Limited transparency== — no mandatory asset disclosure; no clear timelines.

Confidentiality may remain necessary in
rows: Information affecting fair trials or security

items: ==Independent judicial oversight body== — models: UK's ==Judicial Conduct Investigations Office==, European and Latin American judicial councils; revive and empower the lapsed ==Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill, 2010==
==Introduce intermediate sanctions== — US ==Judicial Councils of the Circuits== issue reprimands, suspension or impeachment referral; amend the Judges (Inquiry) Act accordingly
==Statutory timelines== for each stage of removal, preventing evasion by delay
==Close the resignation loophole== — investigations continue and findings are published even after resignation
==Broaden and define ‘misbehaviour’== — corruption, ethical violations, conduct undermining integrity
==Retain senior judges in disciplinary proceedings==, but include ==non-judicial members== for credibility
The Constitution does both: ==security of tenure and fixed salaries== (Arts 124, 125, 217, 221) for independence; ==strict removal procedures== (Arts 124(4), 217(1)(b), 1968 Act) for accountability.
[[Kesavananda Bharati (1973)]] protects independence while ensuring ==constitutional accountability==; [[Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)]] showed both at once.

==Mutual necessity==: an independent judiciary must be accountable to remain legitimate — ==excessive insulation breeds opacity==. [[Sankalchand Sheth]] and [[S.P. Gupta]] reflect early concern for independence; the ==Second Judges Case== established judicial primacy.

==Checks and balances==: independence guards against executive overreach; accountability prevents ==judicial tyranny==. The ==NJAC judgment (2015)== reasserted independence as basic structure but was criticised for ==avoiding structural accountability reforms==.

blocks.text: Constitutional morality rejects the false choice between independence and accountability. Independence without accountability may become judicial supremacy; accountability without independence may become political subordination.
Judicial independence is not a privilege of judges — it is the right of every citizen to an impartial arbiter. Justice must not only be done, but must be seen to be answerable.
